passage: Preeti, you're moving into the hostel next week, so let your Vijay Mama tell you about his first flat in Pune. I shared it with a boy called Mohan. One morning I found a note on the fridge: "Wow, you washed a plate! Should we call the newspapers?" Then another: "Thank you SO much for leaving your socks on the sofa. Very decorative." Every note made my ears go hot. I felt attacked, and I couldn't even argue with a fridge. So I started leaving notes back, sharper ones. Two weeks of paper war. Then my mother said on the phone, "Vijay, ask him what he actually wants." So I did, one evening over chai. Mohan said he was tired of doing the dishes alone. We made a rota. No more notes. So, Preeti, if someone starts writing you notes, go and have chai with them.

qa.a: "Wow, you washed a plate! Should we call the newspapers?"

qa.a: He felt attacked and mocked, with no fair chance to reply, since he couldn't argue with a fridge.

qa.q: What turning point ended the paper war?
qa.a: Following his mother's advice to ask Mohan what he actually wanted, over chai, which led to a dish rota.

qa.q: What might Mohan have been feeling when he wrote the notes?
qa.a: Tired and resentful about doing the dishes alone, but unable or unwilling to say so directly.

It was exam week, the water in their building came for only two hours a day, and Karthik had a thermodynamics paper at nine. At 6 a.m. he found a sticky note on the kettle in Sabina's handwriting: "Thanks SO much for washing your mug. For once. Truly a miracle." Another was stuck to the bucket: "Love how the water fills itself."
Karthik's face burned. He had been up till two studying. He wanted to write something vicious on the back. Instead, before the water came on, he knocked on her door. "Sabina, I saw the notes. I don't want a war before exams. What's bothering you? What do you want me to change?"
She blinked, then sighed. "I've been filling the buckets alone every morning. I'm exhausted too."
They split the mornings: he would take Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays.

"Sure." She didn't look up from her laptop.
"I found this on the fridge." Vikas held up the sticky note. "'Dear Vikas, the pans say thank you for finally meeting you.' And yesterday's, on the kettle."

passage:
Looking back at my first year, the notes were the worst part. My cousin Mahima and I shared a small flat near college, and I was, I admit, not a great dishwasher. But I didn't know she minded until the notes started. "Congratulations on washing ONE spoon! A historic day." Then: "The sink would like to meet you sometime. It's heard so much about you."
I felt ambushed every time I walked into the kitchen. You can't argue with a sticky note. I started coming home late just to avoid them.
Then one evening, instead of writing back something nasty, which I'd already drafted, I knocked on her door. "Mahima, I'm getting the notes. I think you're really fed up. What exactly do you want me to change?"
She went quiet, then said, "Wash up the same night. That's it." We made a rota on an actual piece of paper. Now she calls me "Deepak the Dishwasher", but to my face, and I laugh.

qa.q: What did the second note say about the sink?
qa.a: "The sink would like to meet you sometime. It's heard so much about you."

qa.q: Why did Deepak start coming home late?
qa.a: Deepak felt ambushed and on edge because of notes that couldn't be answered, so avoiding the kitchen seemed easier than facing them.

qa.q: What turning point ended the notes?
qa.a: Deepak knocked instead of sending the nasty reply and calmly asked what Mahima wanted changed, which led to a clear answer and a rota.

qa.q: What might Mahima have been feeling before Deepak knocked?
qa.a: Mahima was likely fed up and resentful about the dishes, but found it easier to hide the anger in sarcastic notes than to say it directly.

passage: I'm Arohi. In second year, my roommate Yamini started leaving sticky notes. First on the fridge: "So glad SOMEONE finished the bread. Thanks!!" Then on my desk: "Loving the new floor decor (your clothes)." Then on the bathroom mirror: "Wow, the tap can turn off! Who knew?" Each one had a smiley face. Each one made my stomach knot. I didn't know how to answer a note. If I wrote one back, it would become a war. If I said nothing, I felt small in my own room. After two weeks, I sat on my bed one evening and said, "Yamini, the notes are really hard for me. They feel like you're angry but I can't answer. What would you like to change?" She went red. Tuesday night

Found another sticky note on the fridge from Tushar: "WOW, the dishes got washed! Mark the calendar!!" And yesterday: "Thanks SO much for leaving your socks in the hall, very decorative."

I actually did wash the dishes this time. I felt attacked. And weird, because what do you reply to? A sticky note? I wrote "Very funny" on one and then tore it up.

Kamal

In the small girls' hostel above the post office in Kodaikanal town, Chandrika came back from the library to a note on her pillow in Alka's round handwriting: "Thank you for gracing our room with your wet towel on my bed. Truly a gift."

It was the third note that week. The first thanked her "for the lovely alarm at 5 a.m." The second praised her "for keeping the light on so artistically till midnight".

Instead she waited until Alka came in with her tea. "Alka, the notes. I get that you're fed up. Can you tell me plainly what you want me to change? I'd actually like to know."

Alka set down her cup, surprised. "The alarm and the light. I have lectures at eight."

"Okay," Chandrika said. "I'll study in the common room after ten, and the alarm goes on vibrate."
